newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - C&W hangs up on Germany.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - C&W hangs up on Germany.

text.p: Britain's Cable and Wireless (C&W) hung up on Germany on Friday.

But while confirming that it was abandoning its German partnership called Vebacom, Britain's second-biggest telecoms group denied that it was effectively pulling out of Europe despite expecting no imminent link-up with a global alliance.

C&W has been tipped as the "perfect partner" for Global One, a marriage between Deutsche Telekom, France Telecom and America's Sprint because it has access to two key markets Global One lacks -- Britain and Asia.
But C&W, whose chief executive Richard Brown is a former Sprint executive, said a deal with Global One or any other such alliance looked some way off.
"We shall only do so if, after careful consideration, we are certain that it will add shareholder value," a spokeswoman said. "In any event, don't expect anything to happen quickly."

Meanwhile, while saying it "talks to people all the time", the company said, "Europe remains a key strategic market for Cable & Wireless, and the company will concentrate its efforts in continental Europe on developing business which will strengthen and support Cable & Wireless Communications' position."
Cable and Wireless Communications is the British-based venture that was formed last year by the merger of four cable companies including C&W's Mercury mobile and networks business.

C&W's decision to drop its deal with utilities Veba and RWE emphasises the enourmous financial clout that telecoms groups need in order to compete effectively in Europe as the markets are eased open to competition in 1998.
C&W says it took fright at Veba's commitment to large-scale infrastrcuture investments in Germany and elsewhere in Europe.
It was also concerned that it would have too little management control of the partnership after C&W and Veba agreed to take RWE on board last year.
The move marks the latest shift in the balance of power as phone groups jockey for position ahead of competition. Some call prices are already falling and some fear margins may follow.

C&W's departure could weaken Vebacom, which hopes to become a serious challenger to Germany's incumbent telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom. And it might boost the competitive position of C&W's arch-rival, British Telecommunications.

BT's has linked up with German conglomerate Viag in a joint venture called Viag Interkom. That alliance, which hopes to become the second operator in Europe's richest telecoms market, was further strengthened on Thursday by recruiting Telenor, the Norwegian state-owned telecoms operator.

While Veba and RWE said in Germany they were seeking a new international partner, some analysts have speculated they may link up with Viag Interkom in a move that would consolidate the German telecoms market and strengthen Telekom's rivals.
To complicate matters, RWE left the Interkom alliance to join Veba and C&W last year.

Terms of C&W's divorce from Veba were welcomed by analysts who rushed to upgrade annual profit forecasts after C&W said the transactions were likely to yield an exceptional pretax profit of around 60 million pounds ($98.5 million) this year.

By selling out its 45 percent interest in the Vebacom GmbH mobile, cable and networks venture for 2.21 billion marks ($1.34 billion), C&W raised a war chest that it will use to cut debt and underpin its development plans across telecoms and cable TV.
The sale was adjusted for C&W's parallel buyout of Veba's half of the much smaller Cable and Wireless Europe SA.

C&W's remaining European operations are relatively small. Cable and Wireless Europe, which has operations in eight European countries, accrued losses of 16 million pounds in the six months to September 30, 1996. ($1=.6097 Pound) ($1=1.6506 Mark)
